lessons.intro: When a table says the fish was lukewarm, the fault is rarely the cook who seared it. It is usually a hand-off: a sauce waiting for a potato, a plate parked on the pass while a server finishes another table. A dish is a relay across stations. If you can trace one plate from the larder to the guest, you can see where minutes and heat leak away, and you can talk to the kitchen in its own terms.

points.p: In the classic brigade each section owns one kind of work. The larder, or garde manger, runs the cold side: salads, terrines, dressings and cold starters. The fish chef breaks down and cooks fish and makes its sauces. The veg chef, the entremetier, covers vegetables, starches, soups and most hot garnishes. The roast chef cooks roast and braised meat and its jus. Pastry is a brigade within the brigade. Smaller kitchens merge these, but the logic holds: components are made in parallel, then brought together at the pass.

Take roast cod with crushed potato and beurre blanc. Hand-off 1: the larder portions the cod and it goes to fish when the order lands. Fish sears and roasts it and finishes the sauce. At the same time veg crushes the potato and wilts the greens. Hand-offs 2 and 3: both arrive at the pass on the same call, not one waiting for the other. Hand-off 4: the pass assembles, checks and wipes the plate, then a server takes it straight to the table. Every arrow is a place where a dish can stall.

The pass is where the kitchen meets the floor. Traditionally the aboyeur called the tickets and set the timings; in most kitchens today the head chef or sous does it. One voice calling keeps the room quiet and the timings joined up. Whoever runs it needs a clear view of every station, a heated pass for the final check and a ticket rail or kitchen screen to pace each table. A cluttered pass, cross-traffic and extra walking are the usual causes of errors and delays.

Your team is the last hand-off. A plate that is perfect on the pass and then waits for a runner has still failed. The fix is agreed rules: who collects, how fast, and what happens when a section is behind. Kitchens test new layouts with a tape walk-through, marking stations on an empty floor and acting out a rush. You can do the same with your runners and the pass.

lessons.atWork: Pick one busy dish this week. Stand by the pass during service and note each hand-off for three tables: when the order is called, when each part arrives, and how long the plate waits for a runner. Share the slowest hand-off with the head chef and agree one change.
lessons.takeaway: A dish is a relay. Know every hand-off, and fix the slowest one, often the last one, between the pass and the table.

lessons.intro: Every month a P&L lands in your inbox, and the eye goes straight to the bottom line. But each line above it answers its own question, and the answers tell you what to change on the floor. Read it top to bottom, always as a share of sales, and it stops being an accountant's page and becomes a list of jobs for next week.

points.p: Menu prices include VAT, so the till total is not your sales. VAT's standard rate is 20%, so divide by 1.2: £120 through the till is £100 of sales. Every percentage on the P&L is measured against that net figure. Sales is broken down into food, drink and other income, and it answers the first question: how much came in, and from where?

points.h: Cost of sales and gross profit
points.p: Cost of sales is what the food and drink you actually used cost. Take it from sales and you have gross profit, the money left to run the site. In our model it is £30, so gross profit is £70, or 70%. That sits between two UK reference points: a 75% gross profit target in one consultant's guide, and the 67% food margin in the UKHospitality and Christie and Co benchmark. If your cost line rises, look at waste, portions, prices and theft, in that order.

Labour is the line a manager controls most directly. In the UK benchmark, payroll was 28.3% of turnover, counting wages, PAYE, National Insurance and managers' salaries. Our model uses £28. It moves with your rota, not your covers, so a quiet Tuesday staffed like a Saturday shows up here. The National Living Wage is £12.71 an hour now and rises 50p to £13.21 in April 2027. One guide works out that 50p on 400 hours a week, with NI and pension, adds £236 a week.

Overheads cover rent, business rates, service charges, energy, repairs, marketing and insurance. Our model puts rent and rates at £10 and everything else at £22. What is left, £10, is EBITDA: earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. That matches the 10% in one UK consultant's example. US guides put net profit, after everything, nearer 3% to 9%, because interest and depreciation still have to come out.

lessons.atWork: Take last month's P&L for one site. Write each line as a percentage of net sales next to the pound figure. Circle the one furthest from the model, then write the question it answers and one action you will take on the floor this week.
lessons.takeaway: Read the P&L as shares of net sales. Each line answers one question, and labour is the line your rota writes.

lessons.intro: Guests do not mark every minute of a meal. They judge a handful of moments and let those stand for the whole night. Jan Carlzon, who turned round Scandinavian Airlines, called them moments of truth. His airline had 10 million customers a year, each meeting about five staff, so the company was in effect created 50 million times a year in those meetings. Your venues are created the same way, one table at a time.

points.p: Carlzon found that the first 15 seconds between a customer and front-line staff set the tone for how the customer sees the whole business. In a restaurant that is the door. One classic research example is a guest waiting at a please-wait-to-be-seated sign for several minutes, which feels longer, before a host appears. Nothing has gone wrong in the kitchen, yet the guest is already irritated. That is why the greeting is the highest peak on the curve.

points.h: Map the steps, then mark the peaks
points.p: A common steps-of-service standard runs: door greeting immediately; server greeting within 1 minute of sitting; first drinks order in 1 to 2 minutes, with drinks back in 2 to 4; a two-bite check-back within 2 minutes of the mains arriving; the bill 2 minutes after dessert plates are cleared; payment handled within 1 minute. Those timings come from a casual-dining guide, so set your own, but notice where they cluster: on the moments guests judge hardest.

On the curve, six moments carry most of the judgement: the booking call, the door greeting, the first drink, the mains and check-back, the bill and payment, and the farewell. Research on hotels lists the same kind of moments: the call to reserve, arrival, being greeted and being looked after. The quieter steps, seating, ordering and clearing, still matter, but a slip there is easier to forgive.

points.h: Staff the peaks, not the shift
points.p: Carlzon gave front-line staff more authority, because a moment of truth cannot wait for a manager. Give the person at each peak the power to fix it on the spot: a host who can offer a drink at the bar if a table is late, a server who can take a dish off the bill. Put your strongest people where the peaks fall in your service, such as the door at 7pm and the bill at 9pm.

lessons.atWork: At tonight's briefing, name the six peaks and give each an owner. For two tables, time the greeting, first drink, check-back and payment against your own standards. Share one peak that slipped and one that shone.
lessons.takeaway: Guests judge a meal on a few moments. Find your peaks, put your best people there, and let them fix problems on the spot.

news.headline: Wednesday is the new night out, with sales up 31% in five years
news.gist: Square data shows Wednesday sales across UK hospitality up 31% since 2021, and up 40% in bars, clubs and lounges.

read.what: Payments firm Square found Wednesday sales in UK hospitality rose 31% over five years, and 40% in bars, clubs and lounges. In its survey of 1,000 business leaders, 44% reported higher Wednesday evening revenue. 47% of under-35s say they go out more on Wednesdays than two years ago. Sheffield's Wednesday sales grew 119%, Newcastle's 62%.
read.how: Guests say smaller crowds (38%) and easier bookings (a quarter) pull them midweek. Operators are leaning in: 56% have added weekday promotions or events, and 41% have changed or expanded menus for midweek guests.
read.soWhat: If your rota still treats Wednesday as a quiet night, you may be understaffed at the peaks that matter. For your own place, a strong midweek trade spreads rent and labour across more covers.
read.take: Pull the last eight Wednesdays' covers and spend per head. If they are climbing, rota for it, and test one Wednesday-only offer.

news.headline: The festive season now runs 12 weeks, into late January
news.gist: UKHospitality says the 12 biggest trading days for food and drink sellers now fall between early November and the last weekend of January.

read.what: Using Square data for the 2025 festive period, UKHospitality says the 12 busiest trading days fell in a 12-week window. The busiest was Saturday 13 December, with transactions up 67% on an average day. The second Saturday in November was up 65%, and the last Saturday in January up 61%. Nearly all 12 were Saturdays.
read.how: The last Friday in November was the only Friday in the top 12, linked to work Christmas parties. Three January Saturdays made the list, and 25% of consumers plan to spend more this festive period.
read.soWhat: This Saturday may be one of your biggest of the season. Christmas planning that starts in December is already late, and January deserves full staffing, not a skeleton rota.
read.take: Mark the second Saturday of November and December and the last Saturday of January as peak days now, with your strongest team on the door and the pass.

news.headline: Pubs set 1 March 2027 for a ban on MPs over hospitality VAT
news.gist: Campaign group Hospitality Voices plans to bar MPs of all parties who have not backed a hospitality VAT cut, from 1 March 2027.

read.what: Hospitality Voices, led by pub operator Andy Lennox, confirmed on 10 November that its ban will start on 1 March 2027. Its online tracker lists more than 300 MPs with no confirmed support for a cut. Unlike an earlier campaign aimed at one party, this one covers MPs of all parties. Venues can sign up on the group's website.
read.how: The group wants an emergency VAT cut for hospitality through a Private Member's Bill. A Westminster Hall debate on hospitality VAT, led by Labour MP Chris Webb, was set for 12 November.
read.soWhat: VAT takes a sixth of every pound through your till, so the rate shapes menu prices and margins. Whether or not a venue joins a ban, the outcome of this campaign matters to anyone pricing a menu.
read.take: Know what a VAT cut would mean for you: divide a typical bill by 1.2 to see your net sales today, and keep an eye on the debate's outcome.

news.headline: Pizza Express brings Houston Hot Chicken to the UK, aiming for 50 sites
news.gist: Pizza Express opened the first UK Houston Hot Chicken in Stevenage, opposite a KFC, and plans 50 UK sites in three years.

read.what: Pizza Express holds the European master franchise for US brand Houston Hot Chicken, which has 27 US sites. The first UK site opened in Stevenage, beside a new Pizza Express. A second is due at the Brunswick Centre in London, and two more are secured. Pizza Express itself has 360 UK sites.
read.how: Chief executive Paula MacKenzie, who spent 11 years at KFC, says spice drives diner choice. The hottest level is about two million Scoville heat units. Some sites will open away from Pizza Express restaurants.
read.soWhat: Big groups are chasing spice and chicken, a small but growing category. It shows how a focused, one-product menu can scale fast, a useful lens when you plan your own concept.
read.take: Look at your menu's heat. Is there one dish with real spice for the guests who choose on it?

news.headline: Henry Lam is the new head chef at China Tang at the Dorchester
news.gist: China Tang has named Henry Lam head chef and launched canapés for events, priced from £32 to £70 a head.

read.what: Henry Lam brings more than 25 years' experience, including Shang Palace at Shangri-La Singapore, the Colony Club in Mayfair, Hakkasan and Canton Blue at the Peninsula London. China Tang, founded in 2005 by the late Sir David Tang, recently marked 20 years. It is run by Lai Sun Dining, whose restaurants hold eight Michelin stars between them.
read.how: The new canapé menu, for receptions, pre-dinner drinks and corporate events, includes black truffle morel spring rolls and sesame prawn toast, at £32 to £70 per person.
read.soWhat: A canapé and events menu turns a famous dining room into a second income stream, sold to corporate clients. It is a model worth costing for any site with a private room.
read.take: Price a three-canapé reception at your venue per head. Would it earn more per hour than a normal table in that room?

news.headline: Public House Group plans its West End debut at 8 Carlos Place, Mayfair
news.gist: The group behind The Pelican has taken a six-storey listed townhouse opposite The Connaught, with consent for a major refit.

read.what: Public House Group, founded by James Gummer, Olivier van Themsche and Phil Winser, has taken 8 Carlos Place, a Grade II-listed townhouse that was Roland Mouret's flagship. Westminster City Council granted planning permission and listed building consent earlier in 2026 for works from the basement to the fourth floor.
read.how: The plans include a second-floor kitchen, new back-of-house areas and toilets, a lift and service lifts, and a new extraction duct. The size could allow several offers under one roof, as the group does in Notting Hill.
read.soWhat: A kitchen on the second floor and service lifts show how much back-of-house a townhouse needs. Read planning documents for sites you like: they show the real cost of a building.
read.take: When you view a site, ask where the kitchen, the extraction and the lift would go before you fall for the front room.

news.headline: Bordelaise brings two-for-one steaks to Dalston Square in January
news.gist: French steakhouse and bistro Bordelaise opens on 5 January in Dalston Square, with about 70 covers inside and a terrace for 50 planned.

read.what: Founder Olivier Cohen's Bordelaise opens in Thomas Tower, Dalston Square, on 5 January, with a terrace planned for spring. The menu runs from onglet, flat iron and rib-eye to onion soup, coq au vin and tarte tatin. Offers include two-for-one steaks, Dorset mussels and fries for £16, and two courses for £19 on set days.
read.how: The first Bordelaise opened in Tooting in 2016 and closed in April after 10 years. The group also runs restaurants in Ewell and Surbiton.
read.soWhat: This is a preview, not yet open. The launch leans on value offers to fill 70 seats in a new area, a common tactic, but one that needs a plan for when the offer ends.
read.take: If you launch with an offer, decide on day one when it ends and what will keep guests coming back after.

news.headline: Claudio Obertelli returns with Torino, three floors at Paddington Square
news.gist: The restaurateur behind Sticky Fingers has opened Torino at 1A Paddington Square: a bakery, a grill restaurant and a rooftop bar, with 49 staff.

read.what: Claudio Obertelli, who built 11 venues across London and New York before selling his group about 10 years ago, has opened Torino with Peter Fulton. The 5,000 sq ft site has a bakery on the ground floor, a grill-led Italian and Mediterranean restaurant on the first floor and a rooftop bar. House wine is £28 a bottle.
read.how: He says pricing is now as big a factor as food, and that a guest should be able to have pasta and a glass of red for much less than £150. He also says finding staff is very difficult.
read.soWhat: One site, three offers from breakfast to late, works hard for its rent. It is a model to study if your own place could trade across the whole day.
read.take: Map your site's trading hours. Which hours earn nothing, and could a second offer fill them?

try.title: Trace one plate and time one table
steps: Before service, pick one popular dish and ask the pass which stations it crosses.
During service, note when it is called, when each part reaches the pass, and how long it waits for a runner.
For one table, time the greeting, first drink, check-back and payment.
After service, share the slowest hand-off and the weakest peak with the team, and agree one fix.
try.why: It joins today's lessons: the plate's hand-offs and the guest's peaks are where a night is won or lost, and both show up later in your labour and sales lines.

quiz.q: A table's fish arrives lukewarm. The cook seared it well and the sauce was hot. Where should you look first?
options: The hand-offs, especially pass to table
quiz.why: A dish is a relay. If the cooking was right, the heat was most likely lost at a hand-off, often while the plate waited on the pass for a runner.

quiz.q: Your till shows £36,000 for the week. What are net sales for the P&L?
quiz.why: Menu prices include VAT at 20%, so divide by 1.2: £36,000 ÷ 1.2 = £30,000. Taking 20% off the till total takes too much.

quiz.q: Covers were flat last month but labour rose from 28% to 32% of sales. What is the most likely cause?
options: Kitchen waste rose across the month
The rota did not match the covers
quiz.why: Labour moves with your rota, not your covers. Supplier prices and waste hit cost of sales, and rent sits in overheads.

quiz.q: Which moment does Carlzon's work suggest sets the tone for a guest's whole view of the business?
options: The first 15 seconds at the door
The farewell as the guest leaves
quiz.why: Carlzon found the first 15 seconds of contact with front-line staff set the tone, which is why the door greeting is the highest peak.

quiz.q: A table's main is late. Under the moments of truth approach, what should happen?
options: The server waits for the manager
The server fixes it on the spot
The kitchen sends a note to the guest
The host moves the next booking
quiz.why: Carlzon gave front-line staff authority because a moment of truth cannot wait for a manager. The person at the peak should be able to fix it there.

terms.def: The counter where each dish's parts are brought together, checked and handed to front of house. It is where the kitchen meets the floor.
The person on the pass who calls the tickets and sets the timings. Today it is usually the head chef or sous chef.
A point where a dish or one of its parts moves from one station or person to the next. Each one is a place where time and heat can be lost.
What the food and drink you actually sold cost you. Taken from net sales, it leaves gross profit.
Net sales minus cost of sales: the money left to pay for labour, overheads and profit. Usually shown as a percentage of sales.
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. The operating profit of a site before financing and accounting charges.
Any contact between a guest and your staff that shapes how the guest judges the whole business. Coined by Jan Carlzon of Scandinavian Airlines.
A quick check with the table soon after the mains arrive, once guests have tasted the food, so problems can be fixed while the meal is still hot.

toolkit.name: Dish trace sheet
items: Dish name and the stations it crosses
Time each part reaches the pass
Time the plate leaves the pass
Slowest hand-off and one fix agreed with the chef

toolkit.name: Six questions for any P&L
items: Sales: how much came in, net of VAT, and from food, drink or other?
Cost of sales: what did the food and drink cost, as a share of sales?
Gross profit: what is left to run the site?
Labour: did the rota match the covers?
Overheads: what do rent, rates, energy and the rest take?
Profit: what is left, and is it before or after interest and depreciation?

toolkit.name: Peak owner card
items: Booking call: who answers, and how fast?
Door greeting: who is on the door at the busiest hour?
First drink: target time from sitting
Mains and check-back: who checks, and when?
Bill and payment: target time from request
Farewell: who says goodbye, every table?
